title: Ἕκτωρ οἴκαδε
about: Achilles tells Priam that Hector has been released and will be his to take at dawn, and urges him to eat, as even Niobe ate when her twelve children lay dead, killed by Apollo and Artemis and then turned to stone herself. He kills a sheep, his men dress and roast it, and the two enemies eat and look at each other with wonder: Priam at Achilles’ size and likeness to a god, Achilles at Priam’s fine bearing and speech. Beds are made on the porch; Achilles teases Priam about the leaders who might find him, asks how many days he needs for the funeral, and grants twelve days of truce, taking the old man’s hand to calm his fear. All sleep but Hermes, who wakes Priam with a warning and drives the wagon through the sleeping camp to the ford of Xanthus, where he leaves them. At dawn the cart reaches Troy with the body of Hector, and Cassandra, on the citadel, sees it first and calls the people to see him.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἐς κλισίην πάλιν ἤϊε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἕζετο δ’ ἐν κλισμῷ πολυδαιδάλῳ ἔνθεν ἀνέστη
τοίχου τοῦ ἑτέρου, ποτὶ δὲ Πρίαμον φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and back into the hut went heavenly Achilles,
and sat down on the richly wrought seat from which he had risen,
by the other wall, and to Priam spoke a word:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and heavenly Achilles went back into the hut and sat down on the richly wrought seat from which he had risen, by the other wall, and said to Priam:
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα ‘he spoke’ closes Achilles’ last words (the previous part) and starts the action; ἤϊε is the Homeric imperfect of εἶμι ‘was going’, and δῖος ‘heavenly’ is Achilles’ stock epithet. κλισίη is the ‘hut’ (shelter-building) of Achilles’ camp, and κλισμός a ‘seat’ (a chair with a back), here πολυδαίδαλος ‘richly wrought’, that is, of much craftsmanship. ἕζετο is ‘sat down’ (ἕζομαι), ἀνέστη the aorist of ἀνίστημι, intransitive, ‘rose’. τοίχου τοῦ ἑτέρου is a genitive of place, ‘by the other wall’; the Greek says only ‘the other’, and does not say which. ποτὶ … φάτο is tmesis: ποτί (= πρός) is parted from φάτο (unaugmented aorist middle of φημί), ‘spoke to’.

sentences.t:
υἱὸς μὲν δή τοι λέλυται γέρον ὡς ἐκέλευες,
κεῖται δ’ ἐν λεχέεσσ’·
sentences.l:
“Your son, indeed, has now been released for you, old man, as you bade,
and lies on a bed;
sentences.i: “Your son has now been released to you, old man, as you asked, and he lies on a bed;
sentences.n: Achilles’ speech begins; the edition prints no quotation marks. υἱὸς μὲν δή is ‘your son, indeed, now’, with τοι ‘for you’ (an enclitic dative of interest) and the perfect passive λέλυται, ‘has been released’ (λύω, the verb of ransom). ὡς ἐκέλευες is ‘as you were bidding’, the imperfect of κελεύω. κεῖται is ‘lies’, and λεχέεσσ’ is the epic dative plural of λέχος ‘bed’; the plural is poetic, for the one bier. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 600.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν
ὄψεαι αὐτὸς ἄγων·
sentences.l:
and with dawn appearing
you will see, yourself leading him away;
sentences.i: at first light you will see, yourself leading him away;
sentences.n: ἅμα … ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν is the formula ‘at first light’, literally ‘with dawn appearing’: ἠοῖ is the dative of ἠώς, and φαινομένηφιν has the old ending -φιν in place of -ῃ. ὄψεαι is the uncontracted future middle of ὁράω, ‘you will see’; αὐτός ‘yourself’ and ἄγων ‘leading, taking away’ stand with it, and the object ‘him’ is understood.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ μνησώμεθα δόρπου.
sentences.l: but now let us think of supper.
sentences.i: Now let us turn our thoughts to supper.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ turns from the body to the meal. μνησώμεθα is the aorist subjunctive middle of μιμνῄσκομαι, ‘take thought of’, a hortatory ‘let us …’, with the genitive δόρπου ‘supper’ (the object of such verbs stands in the genitive).

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ τ’ ἠΰκομος Νιόβη ἐμνήσατο σίτου,
τῇ περ δώδεκα παῖδες ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ὄλοντο
ἓξ μὲν θυγατέρες, ἓξ δ’ υἱέες ἡβώοντες.
sentences.l:
For even fine-haired Niobe took thought of food,
she to whom, indeed, twelve children in the halls perished,
six daughters, and six sons in youthful vigour.
sentences.i: For even fine-haired Niobe took thought of food, though twelve children had perished in her halls, six daughters and six sons in the vigour of youth.
sentences.n: Achilles offers Priam an example, Niobe, whose story he tells to the end of 617. καὶ γάρ τε ‘for even’ introduces it; ἠΰκομος ‘fine-haired’ is her stock epithet; ἐμνήσατο is the aorist of μιμνῄσκομαι, ‘took thought of’, here with the genitive σίτου ‘food’, the same verb as 601. τῇ περ is the relative ‘to whom, indeed’ (the particle περ gives it the force of ‘although’); ὄλοντο is the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι, ‘perished’, and ἡβώοντες the participle of ἡβάω ‘be in youthful vigour’. Line 604 is metrically irregular as transmitted: θυγατέρες needs a lengthened syllable in its second foot, and its last syllable counts long before ἓξ (an older initial w-sound, the digamma, in ἕξ).

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν Ἀπόλλων πέφνεν ἀπ’ ἀργυρέοιο βιοῖο
χωόμενος Νιόβῃ, τὰς δ’ Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα,
οὕνεκ’ ἄρα Λητοῖ ἰσάσκετο καλλιπαρῄῳ·
sentences.i: Apollo killed the sons with shots from his silver bow, angry at Niobe, and Artemis, who showers her arrows, killed the daughters, because Niobe had made herself the equal of fair-cheeked Leto;
sentences.n: The pairing τοὺς μὲν … τὰς δέ ‘those … and these’ is masculine for the sons, feminine for the daughters, and Artemis’ verb is left to be supplied from πέφνεν, ‘killed’ (an unaugmented aorist). βιοῖο is the genitive of βιός ‘bow’ (the accent separates it from βίος ‘life’); χωόμενος is ‘incensed’, with the dative Νιόβῃ ‘at Niobe’. Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα is the house ‘Artemis, who showers her arrows’ (the second half of the epithet is disputed, χέω ‘pour’ or χαίρω ‘delight in’). ἰσάσκετο is an imperfect with the iterative ending -σκ-, ‘kept putting herself on a level with’, taking the dative; καλλιπαρῄῳ ‘fair-cheeked’ is Leto’s epithet here and belongs to Briseis at 676.

sentences.t: φῆ δοιὼ τεκέειν, ἣ δ’ αὐτὴ γείνατο πολλούς·
sentences.l: she said that the two had borne, but she herself had borne many;
sentences.i: She said that Leto had borne two, but that she herself had borne many;
sentences.n: Niobe is the subject of φῆ (imperfect of φημί, ‘she said’); the two are Apollo and Artemis, and Leto is the understood subject of τεκέειν, the aorist infinitive of τίκτω ‘bear’. δοιώ is a dual, ‘two’. ἣ δ’ is ‘but she’, a pronoun, and γείνατο is the aorist middle of γείνομαι ‘bear’. The boast is Niobe’s own, quoted indirectly.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ ἄρα καὶ δοιώ περ ἐόντ’ ἀπὸ πάντας ὄλεσσαν.
sentences.l: but those two, then, though being two, destroyed them all.
sentences.i: but those two, though only two, destroyed them all.
sentences.n: τὼ is a dual demonstrative, ‘those two’, and δοιώ περ ἐόντ’ is ‘two though being’ (a dual participle, ἐόντε elided; περ makes it concessive). ἀπὸ … ὄλεσσαν is tmesis for ἀπώλεσαν, ‘destroyed utterly’; the doubled σ of ὄλεσσαν is the epic form of the aorist. πάντας ‘all of them’ takes in all twelve.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐννῆμαρ κέατ’ ἐν φόνῳ, οὐδέ τις ἦεν
κατθάψαι, λαοὺς δὲ λίθους ποίησε Κρονίων·
sentences.l:
They lay for nine days in slaughter, and there was no one
to bury them, for the people the son of Cronus made stones;
sentences.i: They lay for nine days in their blood, and there was no one to bury them, for the son of Cronus had turned the people to stone;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν ‘they’ are the dead children. κέατ’ is κέατο, the Ionic imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lay’; ἐννῆμαρ ‘for nine days’; φόνος is ‘killing, bloodshed’, so ἐν φόνῳ is ‘in the slaughter’, and the English says ‘in their blood’. οὐδέ τις ἦεν κατθάψαι is ‘nor was there anyone to bury (them)’: κατθάψαι is the aorist infinitive of καταθάπτω, with the prefix assimilated. Κρονίων ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus, and λίθους ‘stones’ is the predicate of ποίησε ‘made’: the people were turned to stone.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ ἄρα τῇ δεκάτῃ θάψαν θεοὶ Οὐρανίωνες.
sentences.l: And them, then, on the tenth day buried the gods, the Uranians.
sentences.i: On the tenth day the gods of heaven buried them.
sentences.n: θάψαν is the unaugmented aorist of θάπτω, ‘buried’ (the same verb as in 611); τῇ δεκάτῃ is ‘on the tenth’, the word ‘day’ left out. Οὐρανίωνες is the house ‘the Uranians’ in the literal layer and ‘the gods of heaven’ in the English: the children or descendants of Ouranos, Heaven, that is, the gods.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἄρα σίτου μνήσατ’, ἐπεὶ κάμε δάκρυ χέουσα.
sentences.l: And she then took thought of food, when she grew weary shedding tears.
sentences.i: And she took thought of food when she had grown weary of shedding tears.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is ‘and she’, a pronoun, and μνήσατ’ is the same aorist ἐμνήσατο as at 602, ‘took thought of’, with σίτου. κάμε is the aorist of κάμνω ‘grow weary’, and the participle χέουσα with δάκρυ is the formula ‘shedding tears’. Niobe eats only when she is exhausted, which is Achilles’ point to Priam.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ που ἐν πέτρῃσιν ἐν οὔρεσιν οἰοπόλοισιν
ἐν Σιπύλῳ, ὅθι φασὶ θεάων ἔμμεναι εὐνὰς
νυμφάων, αἵ τ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀχελώϊον ἐρρώσαντο,
ἔνθα λίθος περ ἐοῦσα θεῶν ἐκ κήδεα πέσσει.
sentences.l:
And now somewhere among the rocks, in the lonely mountains,
in Sipylus, where they say the beds are
of goddesses, of nymphs, who around Achelous danced,
there, though being stone, she cooks sorrows from the gods.
sentences.i: And now, somewhere among the rocks of the lonely mountains, on Sipylus, where they say there are the resting-places of the goddesses, the nymphs who dance around Achelous, there, though a stone, she broods over the sorrows the gods sent her.
sentences.n: Sipylus is a mountain, and Niobe, turned to stone (λίθος περ ἐοῦσα ‘though being stone’), is the rock there. νῦν δέ που is ‘and now, somewhere’, a vague ‘I suppose’; οὔρεσιν is οὔρεσι, the epic dative plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’; οἰοπόλοισιν is usually glossed ‘lonely’, but the sense is not certain. θεάων … νυμφάων are genitive plurals in -άων, ‘of goddesses, of nymphs’, and εὐνάς are ‘beds’, here ‘resting-places’; ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to be’. ἐρρώσαντο is the aorist middle of ῥώομαι, traditionally ‘danced’ (‘moved swiftly’), with ἀμφί + accusative ‘around’; Ἀχελώϊον has the diaeresis. θεῶν ἐκ is ‘from the gods’, with the preposition after its noun. κήδεα are ‘sorrows’ and πέσσει ‘cooks, digests’, the picture of someone turning a grief over and over.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ καὶ νῶϊ μεδώμεθα δῖε γεραιὲ
σίτου·
sentences.l:
But come now, let us two also take thought, heavenly old man,
of food;
sentences.i: But come now, let us two also think of food, heavenly old man;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’, and νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’. μεδώμεθα is the subjunctive middle of μέδομαι, ‘be mindful of’, hortatory, with the genitive σίτου ‘food’. δῖε γεραιέ is a vocative, ‘heavenly old man’: δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet and γεραιός is ‘aged’.

sentences.t:
ἔπειτά κεν αὖτε φίλον παῖδα κλαίοισθα
Ἴλιον εἰσαγαγών·
sentences.l:
afterwards again you may weep for your dear son,
having brought him into Ilios;
sentences.i: afterwards you may weep again for your dear son, when you have taken him into Ilios;
sentences.n: κεν … κλαίοισθα is a potential optative, ‘you may weep’ (κλαίοισθα has the second-person ending -σθα); αὖτε is ‘again’, and φίλον παῖδα is ‘dear son’. εἰσαγαγών is the aorist participle of εἰσάγω ‘lead in’. Ἴλιον is the accusative of motion without a preposition, ‘into Ilios’, the city.

sentences.t: πολυδάκρυτος δέ τοι ἔσται.
sentences.l: and much-wept he will be for you.”
sentences.i: for he will be much wept for.”
sentences.n: πολυδάκρυτος is ‘much-wept’, passive in sense (from δακρύω ‘weep’): the son will be wept for at length, so there is no hurry; the subject ‘he’ is understood. The word is a compound of πολυ- ‘much’ and the verbal adjective of δάκρυ ‘tear’; τοι is ‘for you’ (dative of interest). The closing mark ends Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ ἀναΐξας ὄϊν ἄργυφον ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεὺς
σφάξ’·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and, springing up, a silver-white sheep swift Achilles
slaughtered;
sentences.i: So he said, and swift Achilles sprang up and slaughtered a silver-white sheep;
sentences.n: ἦ καί, ‘he spoke, and’, is the formula that closes a speech and starts the action. ἀναΐξας is the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’; ὄϊν is the accusative of ὄϊς ‘sheep’ (the OCT prints the diaeresis), and ἄργυφον ‘silver-white’ is its epithet. ὠκύς ‘swift’ stands alone with Achilles’ name here (πόδας ὠκύς, ‘swift of foot’, is the fuller phrase of 649). σφάξ’ is the unaugmented aorist of σφάζω, ‘slaughtered’, elided.

sentences.t:
ἕταροι δ’ ἔδερόν τε καὶ ἄμφεπον εὖ κατὰ κόσμον,
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρ’ ἐπισταμένως πεῖράν τ’ ὀβελοῖσιν,
ὄπτησάν τε περιφραδέως, ἐρύσαντό τε πάντα.
sentences.l:
and his companions flayed and dressed it well, in due order,
and cut into pieces skilfully and pierced on spits,
and roasted them very carefully and drew them all off.
sentences.i: and his companions flayed it and dressed it well, in good order, and cut the meat skilfully into small pieces and pierced them on spits, and roasted them with great care, and drew them all off.
sentences.n: The first verbs are imperfects of the work in progress, ἔδερον (δέρω ‘flay’), ἄμφεπον (ἀμφιέπω ‘busy oneself about, dress’) and μίστυλλον (‘cut into small pieces’); πεῖραν is the unaugmented aorist of πείρω ‘pierce’, and ὄπτησαν and ἐρύσαντο ‘roasted’ and ‘drew off’ (from the spits) are aorists. εὖ κατὰ κόσμον is ‘well, in due order’; ὀβελοῖσιν is a dative plural, ‘on spits’. Lines 623–624 also stand in an earlier meal-scene of the Iliad, and the English repeats it.

sentences.t:
Αὐτομέδων δ’ ἄρα σῖτον ἑλὼν ἐπένειμε τραπέζῃ
καλοῖς ἐν κανέοισιν·
sentences.l:
And Automedon, taking bread, dealt it out upon the table
in fair baskets;
sentences.i: Automedon took bread and dealt it out on the table in fair baskets;
sentences.n: Αὐτομέδων is one of Achilles’ men, who serves the bread. ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’; ἐπένειμε is the aorist of ἐπινέμω ‘deal out upon’, with the dative τραπέζῃ ‘the table’. κανέοισιν is the dative plural of κάνεον ‘basket’. The unit stops at the ano teleia in mid-line 626.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ κρέα νεῖμεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l: and the meats distributed Achilles.
sentences.i: and Achilles distributed the meats.
sentences.n: κρέα are ‘meats’ (portions of meat, plural). νεῖμεν is the unaugmented aorist of νέμω ‘distribute’ with the movable ν. The word order puts the verb first and Achilles last, the host’s portion of the work.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: A formula for starting a meal. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα ‘good things’ (the food), ἑτοῖμα ‘ready’ and προκείμενα ‘set before them’ are both neuter plurals agreeing with it, and ἴαλλον is the imperfect of ἰάλλω, ‘sent out, stretched out’: they stretched out their hands.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
ἤτοι Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος θαύμαζ’ Ἀχιλῆα
ὅσσος ἔην οἷός τε·
sentences.i: When they had put from them the desire for drink and food, Priam, a descendant of Dardanus, marvelled at Achilles, at his size and what manner of man he was;
sentences.n: ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο is the formula ‘put away desire’: ἐξ … ἕντο is tmesis, the aorist middle of ἵημι ‘send’, so they sent away their longing. ἤτοι is printed as one word; Δαρδανίδης ‘descendant of Dardanus’ is a patronymic of the family, not of a father, and θαύμαζ’ is the unaugmented imperfect of θαυμάζω ‘marvel at’. ὅσσος ἔην οἷός τε is two indirect questions, ‘how large he was, and what sort (of man)’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 630.

sentences.t: θεοῖσι γὰρ ἄντα ἐῴκει·
sentences.l: for to gods, seen straight on, he was like;
sentences.i: for, seen straight on, he was like the gods;
sentences.n: θεοῖσι is a dative of likeness, ‘to gods’, with ἐῴκει, the pluperfect of ἔοικα used as an imperfect, ‘he was like’. ἄντα is an adverb ‘straight on, directly’: the point is that it is the sight of his face that makes him look like a god. The reason for Priam’s wonder.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ Δαρδανίδην Πρίαμον θαύμαζεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
εἰσορόων ὄψίν τ’ ἀγαθὴν καὶ μῦθον ἀκούων.
sentences.l:
And in turn Achilles marvelled at Dardanus’ descendant Priam,
looking at his good appearance and hearing his speech.
sentences.i: And Achilles in his turn marvelled at Priam, the descendant of Dardanus, as he looked on his good appearance and listened to what he said.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ is ‘but he’ (ὅ is the article used as a pronoun), the second half of the pair begun at 629. εἰσορόων is the participle of εἰσοράω ‘look at’, with the uncontracted -όων; ὄψιν ἀγαθήν is ‘good appearance’ and μῦθον ἀκούων ‘hearing his speech’, the two things that Achilles admires in Priam.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τάρπησαν ἐς ἀλλήλους ὁρόωντες,
τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.l:
But when they had taken their fill of looking at one another,
him first addressed the old man Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: When they had taken their fill of looking at one another, Priam, the old man, godlike in form, spoke to him first:
sentences.n: τάρπησαν is the aorist passive of τέρπω, ‘were satisfied, had enough’; ἐς ἀλλήλους ὁρόωντες is ‘looking at one another’ (ὁρόωντες = ὁρῶντες). τὸν … προσέειπε is the speech-formula with πρότερος ‘first’: Priam speaks before Achilles does. γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής is ‘the old man Priam, godlike in form’ (θεός + εἶδος), the epithet kept every time.

sentences.t:
λέξον νῦν με τάχιστα διοτρεφές, ὄφρα καὶ ἤδη
ὕπνῳ ὕπο γλυκερῷ ταρπώμεθα κοιμηθέντες·
sentences.l:
“Lay me down now as quickly as possible, Zeus-nurtured one, so that now indeed
with sweet sleep we may take our fill, having lain down to rest;
sentences.i: “Put me to bed now as quickly as you can, Zeus-nurtured one, so that we may now at last take our fill of sweet sleep, once we have lain down;
sentences.n: Priam’s speech begins. λέξον is the aorist imperative of λέγω in its old sense ‘lay down, put to bed’, with με ‘me’ as its object; τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’ and διοτρεφές the vocative ‘Zeus-nurtured one’. ὄφρα καὶ ἤδη is ‘so that now indeed’. ταρπώμεθα is the aorist subjunctive of τέρπομαι ‘take one’s fill of’, and ὕπνῳ ὕπο γλυκερῷ is ‘with sweet sleep’ (the preposition follows its noun, so its accent draws back). Line 636 is shared with the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω μύσαν ὄσσε ὑπὸ βλεφάροισιν ἐμοῖσιν
ἐξ οὗ σῇς ὑπὸ χερσὶν ἐμὸς πάϊς ὤλεσε θυμόν,
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ στενάχω καὶ κήδεα μυρία πέσσω
αὐλῆς ἐν χόρτοισι κυλινδόμενος κατὰ κόπρον.
sentences.l:
For not yet have my two eyes closed beneath my eyelids
since at your hands my son lost his life,
but always I groan and cook countless sorrows,
rolling in the enclosures of the courtyard through the dung.
sentences.i: For my eyes have not yet closed beneath their lids since my son lost his life at your hands, but I groan constantly and brood over countless sorrows, rolling about in the enclosures of my courtyard, in the dung.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πω is ‘for not yet’; μύσαν is the aorist of μύω ‘close’, with the dual ὄσσε ‘the two eyes’ taking a plural verb. ἐξ οὗ is ‘from the time when’, and ὑπὸ χερσίν ‘at your hands’. ὤλεσε θυμόν is the house ‘lost his life’ (θυμός as the life that leaves the body). στενάχω ‘I groan’ and κήδεα … πέσσω ‘I cook sorrows’ (that is, brood over them, as Niobe does at 617) are presents. αὐλῆς ἐν χόρτοισι is ‘in the enclosures of the courtyard’ (χόρτος ‘enclosure’); κυλινδόμενος is ‘rolling’ and κόπρον ‘dung’: the grief of a mourner who has thrown himself down on the ground.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὴ καὶ σίτου πασάμην καὶ αἴθοπα οἶνον
λαυκανίης καθέηκα·
sentences.l:
Now at last I have tasted both food and fire-faced wine
have sent down my throat;
sentences.i: Now at last I have tasted food, and let wine that has the look of fire go down my throat;
sentences.n: νῦν δή is ‘now at last’. πασάμην is the aorist of πατέομαι ‘taste, eat’ (with the genitive σίτου ‘food’), and αἴθοπα οἶνον is the house ‘fire-faced wine’ (‘wine that has the look of fire’). λαυκανίης is a genitive of the place through which, ‘down the throat’, and καθέηκα is the aorist of καθίημι ‘send down’, with the uncontracted -έηκα. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 642.

sentences.t: πάρος γε μὲν οὔ τι πεπάσμην.
sentences.l: before this I had in no way tasted.”
sentences.i: until now I had tasted nothing.”
sentences.n: πάρος γε μέν is ‘before this, indeed’, and πεπάσμην the pluperfect of πατέομαι, ‘I had tasted’; οὔ τι ‘in no way’ gives ‘nothing’ with it. The closing mark ends Priam’s speech.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥ’, Ἀχιλεὺς δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἰδὲ δμῳῇσι κέλευσε
δέμνι’ ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ θέμεναι καὶ ῥήγεα καλὰ
πορφύρε’ ἐμβαλέειν, στορέσαι τ’ ἐφύπερθε τάπητας,
χλαίνας τ’ ἐνθέμεναι οὔλας καθύπερθεν ἕσασθαι.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and Achilles to his companions and the handmaids gave orders
to place bedsteads under the portico, and fine blankets,
purple, to throw on, and to spread carpets over them,
and to put in thick cloaks, to wear as covering on top.
sentences.i: So he said, and Achilles ordered his companions and the handmaids to place bedsteads under the portico, throw fine purple blankets on them, spread carpets over the top, and put in thick cloaks to serve as covering on top.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥ’ is ἦ ῥα, ‘he spoke’, closing the speech; ἑτάροισιν ἰδὲ δμῳῇσι is ‘to his companions and to the handmaids’. Four infinitives follow κέλευσε ‘gave orders’: θέμεναι (τίθημι) ‘to place’, ἐμβαλέειν ‘to throw on’, στορέσαι ‘to spread’ and ἐνθέμεναι ‘to put in’; the last clause gives ἕσασθαι, the aorist middle of ἕννυμι, ‘to put on’, so the cloaks are for covering. δέμνια are ‘bedsteads’, ῥήγεα ‘blankets’, τάπητας ‘carpets’, and αἴθουσα is the roofed ‘portico’. Lines 644–646 are shared with the Odyssey (there Helen gives the order for her guests’ bedding).

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ ἴσαν ἐκ μεγάροιο δάος μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσαι,
αἶψα δ’ ἄρα στόρεσαν δοιὼ λέχε’ ἐγκονέουσαι.
sentences.l:
And they went out of the hall with a torch in their hands,
and quickly then spread two beds, bustling about.
sentences.i: And they went out of the hall with a torch in their hands, and quickly made up two beds, working with speed.
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the maidservants. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘they went’; δάος is a ‘torch’, and μετὰ χερσίν ‘in their hands’. στόρεσαν is the aorist of στόρνυμι ‘spread’, and so ‘made up’; δοιὼ λέχε’ (λέχεα) is ‘two beds’ with the dual δοιώ. ἐγκονέουσαι ‘bustling about’ is the house word for hurried work.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπικερτομέων προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: And him, taunting, addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Taunting him, Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction. ἐπικερτομέων is the participle of ἐπικερτομέω, ‘taunt, jeer at’: Achilles’ words that follow are grim play, and the reader is left to judge how far they are in earnest. προσέφη is ‘addressed’, and πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in the feet’ (an accusative of respect) is Achilles’ stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἐκτὸς μὲν δὴ λέξο γέρον φίλε, μή τις Ἀχαιῶν
ἐνθάδ’ ἐπέλθῃσιν βουληφόρος, οἵ τέ μοι αἰεὶ
βουλὰς βουλεύουσι παρήμενοι, ἣ θέμις ἐστί·
sentences.i: “Lie down outside, dear old man, in case one of the Achaeans’ counsellors comes here, those who are always sitting beside me and giving me their counsels, as is the custom;
sentences.n: Achilles’ speech begins. ἐκτὸς … δή is ‘outside, indeed’, and λέξο is the aorist imperative middle of λέγομαι ‘lie down’. μή with the aorist subjunctive ἐπέλθῃσιν is a fear, ‘lest … come’; βουληφόρος is ‘counsel-bearing’, a member of the council. οἵ τέ is ‘who’; βουλὰς βουλεύουσι is a figure of the same root, ‘plan plans’, and παρήμενοι ‘sitting beside’. ἣ θέμις ἐστί is ‘as is the custom’. Achaeans here are the leaders, who come to Achilles for counsel.

sentences.t:
τῶν εἴ τίς σε ἴδοιτο θοὴν διὰ νύκτα μέλαιναν,
αὐτίκ’ ἂν ἐξείποι Ἀγαμέμνονι ποιμένι λαῶν,
καί κεν ἀνάβλησις λύσιος νεκροῖο γένηται.
sentences.l:
If any one of them should see you through the swift black night,
at once he would tell it to Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
and there might be a putting-off of the release of the corpse.
sentences.i: If any of them saw you in the swift black night, he would report it at once to Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, and there might be a delay in the release of the corpse.
sentences.n: τῶν εἴ τίς is ‘if any one of them’, and ἴδοιτο is the aorist optative middle of ὁράω, a remote ‘if he should see’. θοὴν διὰ νύκτα μέλαιναν is the formula ‘through the swift black night’. The answer is αὐτίκ’ ἂν ἐξείποι (aorist optative of ἐξεῖπον ‘tell out’) ‘he would report it at once’; ποιμένι λαῶν is ‘shepherd of the people’, Agamemnon’s epithet. ἀνάβλησις is a ‘putting-off, delay’ and λύσιος the genitive of λύσις ‘release’; κεν … γένηται is an aorist subjunctive, ‘might come about’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
ποσσῆμαρ μέμονας κτερεϊζέμεν Ἕκτορα δῖον,
ὄφρα τέως αὐτός τε μένω καὶ λαὸν ἐρύκω.
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly: for how many days do you intend to hold funeral rites for heavenly Hector, so that for that long I may myself wait and keep the army back.”
sentences.n: The first line is shared with another speech of the Iliad. ἀτρεκέως is ‘exactly’ and κατάλεξον the aorist imperative of καταλέγω ‘recount’; ποσσῆμαρ is ‘for how many days’. μέμονας (perfect of the root of μένος, with present sense ‘you intend’) takes the infinitive κτερεϊζέμεν, from κτερεΐζω ‘perform the rites’ (the κτέρεα, the funeral offerings), and δῖον ‘heavenly’ is Hector’s epithet. ὄφρα τέως is ‘so that for so long’; μένω and ἐρύκω are subjunctives, ‘I may wait’ and ‘I may hold back’, and λαός is the host. The closing mark ends Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: Him then answered the old man Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: Then Priam, the old man, godlike in form, answered him:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction: τὸν ‘him’ is Achilles, and ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής is ‘the old man Priam, godlike in form’ (θεός + εἶδος ‘form’), the epithet kept every time.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δή μ’ ἐθέλεις τελέσαι τάφον Ἕκτορι δίῳ,
ὧδέ κέ μοι ῥέζων Ἀχιλεῦ κεχαρισμένα θείης.
sentences.l:
“If indeed you wish me to accomplish a burial for heavenly Hector,
thus doing, Achilles, you would do pleasing things for me.
sentences.i: “If you are truly willing for me to carry out a burial for heavenly Hector, then in doing so, Achilles, you would do me a pleasing service.
sentences.n: Priam’s speech begins. εἰ μὲν δή is ‘if indeed’; ἐθέλεις takes με as the subject of τελέσαι (the aorist infinitive of τελέω ‘accomplish’), so ‘you are willing that I should …’; τάφον is ‘burial’. ὧδε … ῥέζων is ‘thus doing’ (ῥέζω), and κεχαρισμένα θείης is ‘you would set down things that please’ (an aorist optative with κε), a polite phrase for doing a favour. Ἕκτορι δίῳ is the dative of ‘heavenly Hector’.

sentences.t:
οἶσθα γὰρ ὡς κατὰ ἄστυ ἐέλμεθα, τηλόθι δ’ ὕλη
ἀξέμεν ἐξ ὄρεος, μάλα δὲ Τρῶες δεδίασιν.
sentences.l:
For you know how throughout the town we are shut in, and far off the wood
is to bring from the mountain, and the Trojans are very much afraid.
sentences.i: For you know how we are shut up in the city, and that the wood must be brought from far away, from the mountain, and the Trojans are very much afraid.
sentences.n: οἶσθα γάρ is ‘for you know’; ἐέλμεθα is a perfect passive of εἰλέω, ‘we have been pressed in, are shut up’, and κατὰ ἄστυ ‘throughout the town’. The ὕλη ‘wood’ is the wood for the pyre (the context, not the word, says so), τηλόθι ‘far away’, and ἀξέμεν is an epic infinitive of ἄγω, ‘to bring’, saying what must be done with it. δεδίασιν is the perfect of δείδω, ‘they are afraid’, with present sense; Priam implies that the Trojans are afraid to go out for it.

sentences.t:
ἐννῆμαρ μέν κ’ αὐτὸν ἐνὶ μεγάροις γοάοιμεν,
τῇ δεκάτῃ δέ κε θάπτοιμεν δαινῦτό τε λαός,
ἑνδεκάτῃ δέ κε τύμβον ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ποιήσαιμεν,
τῇ δὲ δυωδεκάτῃ πολεμίξομεν εἴ περ ἀνάγκη.
sentences.l:
For nine days we would lament him in the halls,
and on the tenth we would bury him, and the people would feast,
and on the eleventh we would make a mound over him,
and on the twelfth we shall fight, if indeed there is need.
sentences.i: For nine days we would mourn him in our halls; on the tenth we would bury him, and the people would feast; on the eleventh we would raise a mound over him; and on the twelfth we shall fight, if we must.
sentences.n: Priam sets out the days. ἐννῆμαρ is ‘for nine days’; γοάοιμεν, θάπτοιμεν, δαινῦτο and ποιήσαιμεν are optatives with κε, ‘we would lament, bury, feast (δαίνυμι), make’, a plan put politely as a wish, and the verbs for the last day change to the future πολεμίξομεν, ‘we shall fight’ (the epic form of πολεμίζω). τῇ δεκάτῃ, ἑνδεκάτῃ and δυωδεκάτῃ are ‘on the tenth, eleventh, twelfth’; τύμβον is ‘mound’ and ἀνάγκη ‘necessity’. λαός is the singular ‘people’ with a singular verb.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: And him in turn addressed swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Then swift-footed, heavenly Achilles spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction with αὖτε ‘in turn’. ποδάρκης is Achilles’ epithet ‘swift-footed’ (its formation is uncertain, probably πούς ‘foot’ + ἀρκέω ‘suffice’), and δῖος ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t: ἔσται τοι καὶ ταῦτα γέρον Πρίαμ’ ὡς σὺ κελεύεις·
sentences.l: “This also shall be for you, old Priam, as you bid;
sentences.i: “This too shall be done, old Priam, as you ask;
sentences.n: Achilles’ short speech begins. ἔσται τοι is ‘shall be for you’, and καὶ ταῦτα ‘these things also’ points at the twelve days; γέρον Πρίαμ’ is the vocative, elided, ‘old Priam’. ὡς σὺ κελεύεις is ‘as you bid’.

sentences.t: σχήσω γὰρ πόλεμον τόσσον χρόνον ὅσσον ἄνωγας.
sentences.l: for I shall hold back the war for as long a time as you command.”
sentences.i: for I will hold back the war for as long as you tell me.”
sentences.n: σχήσω is the future of ἔχω in the sense ‘check, hold back’. τόσσον … ὅσσον is ‘for so long … as’ (τόσσον χρόνον ‘so great a time’), and ἄνωγας the perfect with present force, ‘you bid’. The closing mark ends Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἐπὶ καρπῷ χεῖρα γέροντος
ἔλλαβε δεξιτερήν, μή πως δείσει’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, upon the wrist the hand of the old man
he grasped, the right one, lest he be afraid in his heart.
sentences.i: With these words he took the old man’s right hand by the wrist, so that he might not be afraid in his heart.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is ‘so then, having spoken’ (ἄρα, particle ‘then’). ἐπὶ καρπῷ is ‘at the wrist’; χεῖρα … δεξιτερήν is ‘the right hand’, the epithet pulled to the next line. ἔλλαβε is the aorist of λαμβάνω with its λ doubled. μή πως δείσει’ is a negative purpose, δείσει’ being the aorist optative δείσειε of δείδω ‘fear’, ‘lest he be afraid’. A gesture of reassurance after the threat of 650–655.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐν προδόμῳ δόμου αὐτόθι κοιμήσαντο
κῆρυξ καὶ Πρίαμος πυκινὰ φρεσὶ μήδε’ ἔχοντες,
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς εὗδε μυχῷ κλισίης ἐϋπήκτου·
sentences.i: The herald and Priam slept there in the vestibule of the house, each with solid counsels in his wits, but Achilles slept in the innermost part of the well-framed hut;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘these two, then’, answered by αὐτάρ ‘but’ for Achilles. προδόμῳ is the ‘vestibule’ (πρόδομος, the fore-house); αὐτόθι ‘right there’; κοιμήσαντο is the aorist middle of κοιμάω ‘lay down to sleep’. πυκινὰ φρεσὶ μήδε’ ἔχοντες is the formula ‘having solid counsels in their wits’, said in the plural of both men, who are awake with care. μυχῷ is ‘in the innermost part’; ἐϋπήκτου, ‘well-framed’ (εὖ + πήγνυμι ‘fix together’), is the epithet of the hut, the OCT printing the diaeresis. Line 674 is shared with an earlier part of Book 24.

sentences.t: τῷ δὲ Βρισηῒς παρελέξατο καλλιπάρῃος.
sentences.l: and beside him lay Briseis, fair-cheeked.
sentences.i: and beside him lay Briseis, fair-cheeked.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘beside him’ (dative with παρά- in the verb παρελέξατο, the aorist middle of παραλέγομαι ‘lie beside’). Βρισηΐς, with the diaeresis as the OCT prints it, is ‘Briseis’, the woman Achilles was given as his prize. καλλιπάρῃος ‘fair-cheeked’ is her epithet; it was Leto’s at 607.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι μέν ῥα θεοί τε καὶ ἀνέρες ἱπποκορυσταὶ
εὗδον παννύχιοι μαλακῷ δεδμημένοι ὕπνῳ·
sentences.l:
Other gods, indeed, and horse-arming men
were sleeping the whole night through, overcome by soft sleep;
sentences.i: All the other gods and the men armed with horses were sleeping the whole night through, overcome by soft sleep;
sentences.n: ἄλλοι μέν ῥα ‘the others, then’ sets up the exception that comes with ἀλλ’ in 679. ἀνέρες is the epic plural of ἀνήρ ‘men’; ἱπποκορυσταί ‘horse-arming’ is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known (chariot-fighters, or men with horsehair-crested helmets, are the two guesses). εὗδον is the imperfect of εὕδω ‘sleep’, παννύχιοι ‘all night long’, and δεδμημένοι the perfect passive participle of δάμνημι, ‘overcome’. Line 677 also opens Book 2, where it introduces Zeus awake.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐχ Ἑρμείαν ἐριούνιον ὕπνος ἔμαρπτεν
ὁρμαίνοντ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ὅπως Πρίαμον βασιλῆα
νηῶν ἐκπέμψειε λαθὼν ἱεροὺς πυλαωρούς.
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
But Hermes the helper sleep did not seize,
pondering in his heart how Priam the king
from the ships he might send away unseen past the sacred gatekeepers.
He stood then above his head and to him spoke a word:
sentences.i: But sleep did not hold Hermes the helper; he was pondering in his heart how he might send King Priam away from the ships without the sacred gatekeepers seeing. He stood over Priam’s head and spoke to him:
sentences.n: Two sentences make this unit: the first ends at the full stop in 681. ἔμαρπτεν is the imperfect of μάρπτω ‘seize’, and ὁρμαίνοντ’ is the participle ‘pondering’, agreeing with Ἑρμείαν. ἐριούνιος is Hermes’ epithet, translated ‘the helper’; its meaning is not known, and ‘helper’ is one ancient guess. ὅπως with the aorist optative ἐκπέμψειε is ‘how he might send out’, and λαθών ‘unnoticed’ with the accusative ἱεροὺς πυλαωρούς ‘the sacred gatekeepers’ is ‘escaping their notice’. In 682, στῆ is ‘he stood’; ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς does not say whose head, but it is Priam’s; πρὸς … ἔειπεν is tmesis, ‘spoke to’.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον οὔ νύ τι σοί γε μέλει κακόν, οἷον ἔθ’ εὕδεις
ἀνδράσιν ἐν δηΐοισιν, ἐπεί σ’ εἴασεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l:
“Old man, no evil at all is a care to you, that you still sleep
among hostile men, since Achilles has let you be.
sentences.i: “Old man, no harm troubles you at all, that you sleep on among hostile men, now that Achilles has let you be.
sentences.n: Hermes’ speech begins. ὦ γέρον is ‘old man’ (ὦ ‘O’); οὔ νύ τι … μέλει κακόν is ‘no evil is any concern to you’, with σοί γε ‘to you at least’. οἷον ἔθ’ εὕδεις is an exclamatory clause, ‘that you still sleep’, which turns the sentence into a reproach. δήϊος is ‘hostile’ (ἀνδράσιν ἐν δηΐοισιν ‘among hostile men’). εἴασεν is the aorist of ἐάω, ‘allow, let be’: Achilles has not harmed Priam.

sentences.t: καὶ νῦν μὲν φίλον υἱὸν ἐλύσαο, πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκας·
sentences.l: And now, indeed, you have ransomed your dear son, and you gave much;
sentences.i: Now you have ransomed your dear son, and you gave much for him;
sentences.n: καὶ νῦν μέν marks the first half; the second half is πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκας, ‘and you gave much’ (the ransom). ἐλύσαο is the aorist middle of λύω ‘ransom (for oneself)’, φίλον υἱόν ‘your dear son’.

sentences.t:
σεῖο δέ κε ζωοῦ καὶ τρὶς τόσα δοῖεν ἄποινα
παῖδες τοὶ μετόπισθε λελειμμένοι, αἴ κ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
γνώῃ σ’ Ἀτρεΐδης, γνώωσι δὲ πάντες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
but for you alive even three times as much ransom would give
the sons who are left behind, if Agamemnon
Atreus’-son should recognise you, and all the Achaeans recognise you.”
sentences.i: but for your life your sons who are left behind would give three times as much ransom, if Agamemnon, son of Atreus, should recognise you, and all the Achaeans should recognise you.”
sentences.n: σεῖο … ζωοῦ is a genitive of price, ‘for you alive’ (ζωός is the epic ‘alive’). καὶ τρὶς τόσα is ‘even three times as much’; δοῖεν is the aorist optative of δίδωμι ‘they would give’, with ἄποινα ‘ransom’. τοὶ is the article used as a demonstrative, ‘those’; μετόπισθε λελειμμένοι is ‘left behind’ (the perfect passive participle of λείπω), Priam’s remaining sons. αἴ κ’ is εἰ κε ‘if’, with the aorist subjunctives γνώῃ and γνώωσι ‘should recognise’. Ἀτρεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Atreus’. The closing mark ends Hermes’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ἔδεισεν δ’ ὃ γέρων, κήρυκα δ’ ἀνίστη.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid, and he made the herald rise.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid and woke the herald.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech, and ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ uses the article as a pronoun. ἔδεισεν is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’ (the verb Achilles meant to calm at 672). ἀνίστη is the imperfect of ἀνίστημι in its transitive sense ‘made stand up’, hence ‘woke’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἑρμείας ζεῦξ’ ἵππους ἡμιόνους τε,
ῥίμφα δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτὸς ἔλαυνε κατὰ στρατόν, οὐδέ τις ἔγνω.
sentences.l:
and for them Hermes yoked the horses and mules,
and swiftly himself drove through the army, and no one recognised them.
sentences.i: and for them Hermes yoked the horses and mules, and drove swiftly through the camp himself, and no one recognised them.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is a dative of advantage, ‘for them’, the herald and Priam. ζεῦξ’ is the aorist of ζεύγνυμι ‘yoke’, ἔλαυνε the imperfect of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’; ῥίμφα is ‘swiftly’. αὐτός ‘himself’ stresses that the god is the driver. οὐδέ τις ἔγνω is ‘and no one recognised (them)’; ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω, the verb of 688.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πόρον ἷξον ἐϋρρεῖος ποταμοῖο
Ξάνθου δινήεντος, ὃν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς,
Ἑρμείας μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀπέβη πρὸς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον,
sentences.l:
But when now the ford they reached of the fair-flowing river,
of eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot,
Hermes then went away to long Olympus,
sentences.i: But when they came to the ford of the fair-flowing river, eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot, Hermes then went off toward tall Olympus,
sentences.n: A when-clause with its main clause in 694; the unit stops at the comma because the whole sentence runs past four lines. ἷξον is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’; πόρον is ‘ford’, and ἐϋρρεῖος ‘fair-flowing’, δινήεντος ‘eddying’ are the river’s epithets. ὃν … τέκετο is the aorist middle of τίκτω, ‘whom (Zeus) begot’; ἀθάνατος ‘immortal’. ἀπέβη is ‘went away’ and μακρόν ‘long’, ‘tall’. Lines 692–693 and 694 are shared with earlier parts of the poems.

sentences.t:
Ἠὼς δὲ κροκόπεπλος ἐκίδνατο πᾶσαν ἐπ’ αἶαν,
οἳ δ’ εἰς ἄστυ ἔλων οἰμωγῇ τε στοναχῇ τε
ἵππους, ἡμίονοι δὲ νέκυν φέρον.
sentences.i: and Dawn in her saffron robe was spreading over all the earth, while they drove the horses to the city, with wailing and groaning, and the mules carried the corpse.
sentences.n: Ἠὼς … κροκόπεπλος ‘saffron-robed Dawn’ is the stock epithet of Dawn, and ἐκίδνατο the imperfect middle of κίδνημι ‘was spreading’. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are Priam and the herald; ἔλων is the participle ‘driving’, whose object is ἵππους ‘the horses’, set at the start of 697. οἰμωγῇ τε στοναχῇ τε are two datives, ‘with wailing and with groaning’. ἡμίονοι δὲ νέκυν φέρον is ‘and the mules carried the corpse’, φέρον the imperfect of φέρω: the mules draw the wagon with Hector on it.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
ἔγνω πρόσθ’ ἀνδρῶν καλλιζώνων τε γυναικῶν,
sentences.l:
and no one else
recognised them first, of men and of fair-girdled women,
sentences.i: and no one else, of men or of fair-girdled women, recognised them first,
sentences.n: οὐδέ τις ἄλλος ἔγνω is ‘and no one else recognised’, the verb of 691; ἀνδρῶν … γυναικῶν is a partitive genitive, ‘of men and of women’. πρόσθ’ is ‘before’ (πρόσθε), with the sense ‘first, before her’, which the next unit supplies. καλλιζώνων ‘fair-girdled’ is the stock epithet of women. The unit ends at a comma because the sentence would otherwise run to five lines.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄρα Κασσάνδρη ἰκέλη χρυσῇ Ἀφροδίτῃ
Πέργαμον εἰσαναβᾶσα φίλον πατέρ’ εἰσενόησεν
ἑσταότ’ ἐν δίφρῳ, κήρυκά τε ἀστυβοώτην·
sentences.i: But Cassandra, who was like golden Aphrodite, went up to Pergamus and caught sight of her dear father standing in his chariot, and the herald, the town-crier;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄρα ‘but then’ brings in the exception: Κασσάνδρη is Priam’s daughter, the prophetess. ἰκέλη χρυσῇ Ἀφροδίτῃ is ‘like golden Aphrodite’. Πέργαμον is Pergamus, the citadel of Troy; εἰσαναβᾶσα is the aorist participle ‘having gone up into’, and εἰσενόησεν ‘caught sight of’. ἑσταότ’ is the perfect participle of ἵστημι ‘standing’; δίφρῳ is here the ‘chariot’. ἀστυβοώτης is ‘town-shouter’ (ἄστυ + βοάω ‘shout’), a herald who cries to the town.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ἐφ’ ἡμιόνων ἴδε κείμενον ἐν λεχέεσσι·
sentences.l: and him upon the mules she saw, lying on a bed;
sentences.i: and she saw him lying on a bed upon the mule-wagon;
sentences.n: τὸν is Hector. ἐφ’ ἡμιόνων is ‘upon the mules’, the wagon they draw being left to be understood, and ἴδε is the aorist of ὁράω ‘saw’. ἐν λεχέεσσι is ‘on a bed’, the poetic plural again for one bier (see 600).

sentences.t: κώκυσέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα γέγωνέ τε πᾶν κατὰ ἄστυ·
sentences.l: and she cried out then, and called aloud all through the town:
sentences.i: She cried out, and called aloud through the whole town:
sentences.n: κώκυσε is the aorist of κωκύω ‘shriek, cry out’; γέγωνε is a perfect with present force, ‘she called aloud’ (γεγωνέω). πᾶν κατὰ ἄστυ is ‘all through the town’. The colon announces her speech.

sentences.t:
ὄψεσθε Τρῶες καὶ Τρῳάδες Ἕκτορ’ ἰόντες,
εἴ ποτε καὶ ζώοντι μάχης ἐκνοστήσαντι
χαίρετ’, ἐπεὶ μέγα χάρμα πόλει τ’ ἦν παντί τε δήμῳ.
sentences.i: “Come and see Hector, Trojans and Trojan women, if ever you rejoiced when he came home alive from battle; for he was a great joy to the city and to all the people.”
sentences.n: Cassandra’s speech. ὄψεσθε is the future ‘you will see’, used with ἰόντες ‘going’ as a summons: ‘go and see’. Τρῳάδες are ‘Trojan women’. εἴ ποτε is ‘if ever’, and χαίρετ’ is ‘you rejoiced’ (an imperfect without its augment), with the datives ζώοντι ‘at him living’ and μάχης ἐκνοστήσαντι ‘come home from battle’ (ἐκνοστέω ‘come home out of’); καί ‘even’ stresses that he was alive. χάρμα is ‘joy’, and δήμῳ ‘people’; πόλει τ’ … παντί τε δήμῳ ‘to the city and to the whole people’. The closing mark ends Cassandra’s speech and the part.
